title: Climbing the Hill
subtitle: how a computer finds the top
name: ModelInMotion_LogisticFE_E07_ClimbingTheHill
status: DRAFT: script under review together with its animatic.

segments.visual: Episode 6's hill, its top marked. A climber's dot waits at the foot with a question mark.

sentences.text: Last time we found the top of the hill: the one setting where every meter that can level is level.
But we found it by being told where it was.

segments.visual: The balance equation for one clinic, with the S-curve inside it. A label: no formula solves this.

sentences.text: A computer has no such luck. It cannot solve for the top with algebra, because every expected count passes through the S-curve.
All it can do, from wherever it stands, is feel the ground: which way is up, and how the slope is changing.

segments.visual: Two small marks at the climber's feet: a slope arrow and a curvature arc.

sentences.text: So how do you climb a hill you can only feel one spot at a time?

segments.visual: Series logo and wordmark; arc and episode title.

sentences.text: Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: climbing the hill.

segments.visual: Dune's slider alone, standing at −1.52. The dial is held at 2.02.

sentences.text: Start small, with one slider. Hold the dial at its fitted place, 2.02, and stand Dune's slider in the wrong spot: on Cedar's level, minus 1.52.
sentences.say: Start small, with one slider. Hold the dial at its fitted place, two point zero two, and stand Dune's slider in the wrong spot: on Cedar's level, minus one point five two.

segments.visual: Dune's own hill, drawn faintly: its height for every slider position. A dot marks where we stand.

sentences.text: Here is Dune's own hill: its height for every position of its slider.
From where we stand, we can't see it. We know just two things: the slope under our feet, and how fast that slope is changing.

segments.visual: A parabola through the dot, matching the hill there. Its top is marked: 0.96 to the right, at −0.56. The dot jumps to it.

sentences.text: That is enough to draw a parabola that matches the hill right here.
So jump to the top of the parabola: 0.96 to the right, to minus 0.56.
sentences.say: So jump to the top of the parabola: zero point nine six to the right, to minus zero point five six.

segments.visual: A second, much smaller parabola: 0.017 to the left. The dot settles at −0.58, the top of Dune's hill.

sentences.text: Do it again from the new spot. The second jump is tiny: 0.017 back to the left.
sentences.say: Do it again from the new spot. The second jump is tiny: zero point zero one seven back to the left.

sentences.text: And we are there: minus 0.58. Two steps.
sentences.say: And we are there: minus zero point five eight. Two steps.

segments.visual: Dune's meter, large: observed 7, expected 4.8, a gap of 2.2.

sentences.text: Where did 0.96 come from? Read it off the meter.
sentences.say: Where did zero point nine six come from? Read it off the meter.

sentences.text: The tilt, we know: observed 7, expected 4.8, a gap of 2.2.
sentences.say: The tilt, we know: observed seven, expected four point eight, a gap of two point two.

segments.visual: A hump: how much each patient adds to the wobble, against their probability. Marks at 18% and 62%, Dune's two groups; the sum, 2.29.

sentences.text: The second number is how readily the expected count moves when the slider does. Call it the wobble.
A patient near 50% adds the most to it. A patient near 0 or near 100% hardly adds at all.
sentences.say: A patient near fifty percent adds the most to it. A patient near zero or near a hundred percent hardly adds at all.

sentences.text: For Dune's twelve patients, it comes to 2.29.
sentences.say: For Dune's twelve patients, it comes to two point two nine.

segments.visual: The step as a fraction: tilt over wobble, 2.2 over 2.29, equals 0.96.

sentences.text: So the step is tilt over wobble: 2.2 divided by 2.29.
sentences.say: So the step is tilt over wobble: two point two divided by two point two nine.

sentences.text: A gap of 2.2 to close, at 2.29 per unit of slider: move 0.96.
sentences.say: A gap of two point two to close, at two point two nine per unit of slider: move zero point nine six.

segments.visual: Caption: which way, and how far.

sentences.text: That division is what makes this more than walking uphill. It does not just say which way. It says how far.

segments.visual: The whole machine at the plain guess. All five sliders step at once.

sentences.text: Now the whole machine, from the plain guess. Every clinic can take its step at the same moment, because each step uses only that clinic's own patients.

segments.visual: The dial steps; the clinic meters tilt again. Sliders, dial, sliders: a round counter ticks.

sentences.text: Then the dial takes one step, with the sliders frozen.
But that unsettles every clinic, so the sliders step again. Then the dial. Then the sliders.

segments.visual: The round counter reaches 8 with the dial at 1.91; then runs on to 54, where the meters are level.

sentences.text: Watch the dial. After eight rounds it has only reached 1.91, on its way to 2.02.
sentences.say: Watch the dial. After eight rounds it has only reached one point nine one, on its way to two point zero two.

sentences.text: Each round covers a fraction of what is left. Getting there takes 54 rounds.
sentences.say: Each round covers a fraction of what is left. Getting there takes fifty-four rounds.

sentences.text: And Elm steps down by about one unit every round, without end.

segments.visual: The hill from above: the dial left to right, Birch's slider up and down, contour lines around the top. The path appears as a staircase.

sentences.text: Here is why it is slow. This is the hill seen from above: the dial runs left to right, Birch's slider up and down.
The path is a staircase: up or down for the sliders, sideways for the dial.

segments.visual: The ridge is drawn as a dashed diagonal through the top.

sentences.text: And the ridge it is trying to follow runs diagonally. Turn the dial up, and every expected count rises, so every slider has to come down.
A staircase is a slow way along a diagonal.

segments.visual: Three rows beside the map: zero at a lower-risk patient, 54 rounds; zero five units away, 3,125 rounds.

sentences.text: How slow depends on something that should not matter: where we put zero.
Last episode, moving zero changed every gamma and no gap. It changes the climb too.
Record the risk factor five units higher, and the same alternation needs 3,125 rounds.
sentences.say: Record the risk factor five units higher, and the same alternation needs three thousand one hundred and twenty-five rounds.

segments.visual: The third row: zero in the middle of the patients, 21 rounds, with the package's name.

sentences.text: Put zero in the middle of the patients instead, and the ridge straightens: 21 rounds. That is what pprof_py does before it starts.
sentences.say: Put zero in the middle of the patients instead, and the ridge straightens: twenty-one rounds. That is what p-prof pie does before it starts.

segments.visual: Three recap cards, each with a small icon.

sentences.text: Let's gather it up.
A step is tilt over wobble. It says which way, and how far.
The sliders can all step at once. The dial steps in turn.
And taking turns climbs a diagonal ridge by staircase.

segments.visual: A line under the cards: every route climbs toward the same top.

sentences.text: Every route here climbs toward the same top. They differ in how long they take.

segments.visual: The map again, with one straight arrow along the ridge to the top; the next episode's title.

sentences.text: So here is the obvious question. Could the sliders and the dial step together, straight along the ridge?
They can, and then it takes five steps. Next time: the arrow matrix.

segments.visual: Series end card with the next episode title.

sentences.text: This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
